courses.title: Orthodontics and Paediatric Dentistry
courses.description: Growth of the face, malocclusion classification and diagnosis, orthodontic appliances, and dental care of children including behaviour management, caries prevention, pulp therapy and trauma.

topics.title: Craniofacial Growth and Development of Occlusion
topics.summary: Growth mechanisms, development of the dentition, and space in the arches.

material.heading: Growth
material.body: Craniofacial growth follows a cephalocaudal gradient: the cranium (neural pattern) grows early and is nearly complete by about 7 years; the face (general/somatic pattern) grows later with a pubertal growth spurt (girls about 11–13 years, boys about 13–15 years). Growth mechanisms: sutural growth (maxilla — displaced downwards and forwards), surface remodelling (deposition and resorption), endochondral ossification at the cranial base synchondroses and mandibular condyle, and displacement. The mandible grows mainly by condylar growth and ramus remodelling, and continues growing later than the maxilla (mandibular prognathism can worsen after puberty). Timing of treatment uses growth indicators (cervical vertebral maturation, hand–wrist radiographs). Functional appliances are most effective during the pubertal growth spurt.

material.heading: Development of the dentition
material.body: The primary dentition ideally shows spacing (primate spaces — mesial to upper canines and distal to lower canines) to accommodate larger permanent incisors; a flush terminal plane, mesial step or distal step relationship of primary second molars predicts the permanent molar relationship. The mixed dentition: first permanent molars erupt at 6 years, incisors 6–8, canines and premolars 10–12, second molars 12. The 'ugly duckling' stage (distally flared upper incisors with a midline diastema at 8–10 years) is normal and resolves as canines erupt. Leeway space (the difference in size between primary canines/molars and their successors — about 1.5 mm per side in the maxilla and 2.5 mm per side in the mandible) allows molar adjustment. Premature loss of primary molars causes space loss and crowding — space maintainers may be needed. Maxillary canines should be palpable buccally by 10–11 years; if not, suspect palatal impaction.

topics.title: Malocclusion: Classification and Diagnosis
topics.summary: Angle's and incisor classification, aetiology, IOTN and orthodontic assessment.

material.heading: Classification
material.body: Angle's classification (molars): Class I (mesiobuccal cusp of the upper first molar occludes in the buccal groove of the lower first molar), Class II (lower molar distal) and Class III (lower molar mesial). The British Standards incisor classification: Class I (lower incisor edges occlude on or below the cingulum plateau of the upper incisors), Class II division 1 (increased overjet with proclined upper incisors), Class II division 2 (retroclined upper central incisors, deep overbite), Class III (lower incisor edges anterior to the cingulum plateau — reduced or reversed overjet). Other features: overjet (normal 2–4 mm), overbite (normal about one-third coverage), open bite (digit sucking, tongue thrust), crossbite (anterior or posterior — with mandibular displacement), crowding and spacing, and centreline discrepancies. Bimaxillary proclination is relatively common in Nigerian and other African populations and may be an ethnic norm.

material.heading: Aetiology and assessment
material.body: Aetiology: skeletal pattern (anteroposterior, vertical and transverse), soft tissues (lips, tongue), dental factors (tooth–arch size discrepancy, hypodontia, supernumeraries, early loss of primary teeth), and habits (digit sucking causing anterior open bite, increased overjet and posterior crossbite). Assessment: history (motivation, medical and dental history), extraoral examination (profile, facial proportions, lips, TMJ), intraoral examination, study models, radiographs (OPG, lateral cephalogram — ANB angle: normal 2–4°; > 4° Class II skeletal, < 2° Class III skeletal). Need for treatment is assessed with the Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need (IOTN — dental health component grades 1–5, with the MOCDO hierarchy: Missing teeth, Overjet, Crossbites, Displacements, Overbite; and an aesthetic component). Treatment aims include function, aesthetics, stability and dental health; risks include decalcification, root resorption, relapse and poor cooperation.

topics.title: Orthodontic Appliances and Treatment
topics.summary: Removable, functional and fixed appliances, extractions, anchorage and retention.

material.heading: Appliances
material.body: Removable appliances (acrylic baseplate with Adams clasps for retention, springs for tipping movements, bite planes) are limited to simple tipping movements and require compliance. Functional appliances (twin block, Fränkel, activator) posture the mandible forwards to correct Class II malocclusions in growing children. Fixed appliances (brackets bonded to teeth, archwires — nickel–titanium for initial alignment, stainless steel for later stages, elastics) achieve precise three-dimensional movements (bodily movement, torque, rotation). Clear aligners are increasingly used for mild to moderate cases. Biology of tooth movement: pressure on one side of the periodontal ligament causes osteoclastic bone resorption; tension on the other stimulates deposition; light continuous forces are ideal (heavy forces cause hyalinisation and root resorption). Headgear and temporary anchorage devices (mini-screws) reinforce anchorage.
keyPoints: Functional: Class II in growing children

material.heading: Treatment planning and retention
material.body: Space for correction may come from extractions (commonly premolars), interproximal enamel reduction, arch expansion (rapid maxillary expansion splits the midpalatal suture in growing patients for posterior crossbites), distalisation of molars, or proclination of incisors. Anchorage is resistance to unwanted tooth movement. Interceptive orthodontics includes correcting anterior crossbites early, extracting retained primary teeth, space maintenance, habit breaking (e.g. habit-breaking appliances for thumb sucking), and extracting primary canines to encourage eruption of palatally displaced permanent canines. Severe skeletal discrepancies in adults require combined orthodontics and orthognathic surgery (e.g. bilateral sagittal split osteotomy, Le Fort I osteotomy). Retention after treatment is essential because teeth tend to relapse (gingival fibres, soft tissue pressures, growth): removable retainers (Hawley, vacuum-formed) and bonded fixed retainers; long-term retention is now recommended.

topics.title: Paediatric Dentistry: Behaviour and Prevention
topics.summary: Child behaviour management, caries risk and prevention, fluoride and sealants.

material.heading: Behaviour management
material.body: Children's cooperation depends on age, previous experiences, parental anxiety and the dental team's approach. Non-pharmacological techniques: tell–show–do, positive reinforcement (praise), voice control, distraction, modelling, and parental presence/absence as appropriate; build rapport and use child-friendly language. Pharmacological options: inhalation sedation with nitrous oxide/oxygen (relative analgesia — safe, rapid onset and recovery), oral or intravenous sedation (specialist settings), and general anaesthesia for extensive treatment in very young or uncooperative children or those with special needs. The Frankl scale rates behaviour from definitely negative to definitely positive. Children with special health care needs (cerebral palsy, autism, Down syndrome, sickle cell disease, heart disease, bleeding disorders) need tailored care and prevention. Safeguarding: dentists must recognise signs of child abuse and neglect (dental neglect, facial injuries) and act.

material.heading: Prevention
material.body: Early childhood caries (any caries in a child under 6; severe forms affect upper incisors and molars; associated with frequent sugary drinks, night-time bottle feeding with sweetened liquids, and poor oral hygiene) is common in urban Nigerian children. Prevention: parental supervision of twice-daily brushing with fluoride toothpaste (a smear/rice-grain size for under-3s with 1,000 ppm; pea-sized for 3–6 years with 1,000–1,450 ppm; spit, don't rinse), reducing frequency of sugar intake, avoiding sweetened drinks in bottles at night, professional fluoride varnish (22,600 ppm; 2–4 times per year for high-risk children), and fissure sealants on permanent molars soon after eruption. Water fluoridation is not established in Nigeria; excessive fluoride (in some borehole water) causes fluorosis. Anticipatory guidance at the first dental visit (by age 1) and school oral health programmes are recommended.

topics.title: Paediatric Pulp Therapy and Dental Trauma
topics.summary: Pulpotomy and pulpectomy in primary teeth, stainless steel crowns, and managing dental injuries in children.

material.heading: Pulp therapy in primary teeth
material.body: Primary teeth have large pulps, thin enamel and dentine, and caries spreads quickly. Treatment options: indirect pulp capping, pulpotomy (removal of inflamed coronal pulp in vital primary molars with carious exposure; medicaments — MTA, Biodentine, ferric sulfate; formocresol historically), pulpectomy (removal of all pulp in non-vital or irreversibly inflamed primary teeth with resorbable fill — zinc oxide eugenol or iodoform pastes such as Vitapex), and extraction (with space maintenance when needed). Preformed metal (stainless steel) crowns are the most durable restoration for primary molars after pulp therapy or with multi-surface caries; the Hall technique seals caries without local anaesthesia or preparation. In young permanent teeth with open apices, preserve pulp vitality (apexogenesis via partial pulpotomy — Cvek) to allow continued root development; necrotic immature teeth need apexification (MTA barrier) or regenerative endodontics.
keyPoints: Pulpotomy for vital exposed primary molars

material.heading: Dental trauma
material.body: Dental injuries are common in children (falls, play, sports, road crashes, abuse — check consistency of history). Upper central incisors are most affected; increased overjet with lip incompetence increases risk. Classification (Andreasen): enamel and enamel–dentine fractures (restore, preserve fragment reattachment), complicated crown fractures with pulp exposure (pulp capping or partial pulpotomy), root fractures, and luxation injuries (concussion, subluxation, extrusion, lateral luxation, intrusion) and avulsion. Avulsed permanent teeth: replant immediately if possible (hold by the crown, rinse with milk or saline, reinsert) or store in milk, saliva or saline; flexible splint for 2 weeks; antibiotics and tetanus status; root canal treatment within 7–10 days for teeth with closed apices. Never replant avulsed primary teeth (risk to the permanent successor). Primary tooth intrusion may damage developing permanent teeth (enamel hypoplasia — Turner's tooth). Mouthguards prevent sports injuries. Follow the International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines.
